newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda says former Hutu army running east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda says former Hutu army running east Zaire.

text.p: Rwanda's military strongman said on Tuesday his country's former Hutu army and militiamen were "running the show" in war-torn eastern Zaire and he had reports of widescale massacres there.
Independent sources confirmed the ex-Rwandan army was in alliance with Zairean government forces in the beleaguered city of Bukavu but denied it was in charge.

Rwandan Vice President and Defence Minister Major-General Paul Kagame, a Tutsi, told Reuters that Hutu soldiers of the 45,000-strong former Rwandan army (FAR) were effectively running Bukavu and Goma, the main cities in eastern Zaire.

"It is clear they (former Rwandan soldiers and militiamen) are now running the show in eastern Zaire. If they are allowed to continue reigning over that region then the implications will be far-reaching," he said in an interview in Kigali.

He said the Rwandans, who fled their homeland in 1994 after leading the genocide of minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus, had control of Goma and Bukavu after Zairean troops fled from advancing ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels.
But independent sources, including foreign journalists in Bukavu, said Kagame's assertion was an exaggeration.
"A FAR general is now taking part in military briefings with the senior Zairean officers in Bukavu," one source who arrived in Nairobi on Monday and declined to be quoted by name told Reuters.
He said FAR men had been sighted in Bukavu and there were reports of a checkpoint at one entrance to the city jointly manned by Zairean and Rwandan Hutu militiamen.
"But the FAR are by no means in sole control," he said.
There was no evidence that FAR men were in charge of Goma, the main base in the east for Zaire's ragged army.

Kagame, who led the Tutsi-dominated Rwanda Patriotic Front (RPF) rebels to victory in 1994 against Hutu forces behind the genocide, said he had intelligence reports of widescale massacres of Zaireans and Zaireans of Rwandan origin.
"I don't know how far this can be allowed to go on. It is a dangerous precedent if we allow people to be uprooted from their homes and massacred on the basis of ethnicity," Kagame said.
He said indigenous Zaireans and Zaireans of Rwandan origin were being systematically arrested and 500 Tutsis had disappeared from Goma, the capital of North Kivu province.
Sources in Bukavu said there were no ethnic Tutsis left there. They have fled, been killed, or are in hiding.

The Banyamulenge, from a 300,000-strong Tutsi community that migrated from what is now Rwanda to Zaire up to 200 years ago, have captured towns south of Bukavu and are thought to be as close as 15 km (10 miles) from the city.
Indigenous Zaireans who fled into Rwanda spoke on Monday of widespread killings, looting and rapes by the Zairean army and Rwandan Hutu militiamen.
Kagame described the situation in the cities of Bukavu and Goma to the north as "completely chaotic and out of control".

He ruled out a regional war in the Great Lakes area of central Africa because of the crisis but, under persistent questioning, said full-scale confrontation between Zaire and Rwanda could not be ruled out if ethnic cleansing continued.
"We will be the last people to open fire but one sees it coming in view of what is happening," he said.
He accused the international community of doing nothing while innocent people were being massacred in Zaire and said it resembled the situation during the genocide in Rwanda in 1994.

"It is happening again and once again the international community is silent on the matter," said Kagame. The Rwandan government has repeatedly denied Zairean accusations that its troops are fighting alongside Tutsi rebels in eastern Zaire.
Brian Atwood of the U.S. Agency for International Development said in Washington on Monday it appeared Rwandan military forces helped Tutsi rebels in their weekend offensive in the Goma region.
